items.content_text: Thinking, Fast and Slow, Part 3. Overconfidence A good story makes the base rates disappear. Kahneman opens this part with the Google origin story. Two Stanford grad students, a better search algorithm, and a company worth more than most countries. The pieces connect, so the ending feels earned. He even includes the lucky break, the year the founders tried to sell the whole thing for under a million dollars and the buyer thought that was too much. The detail makes the story better, and it makes the other luck easier to miss. Part 2 covered what the mind does to numbers. This part is about what WYSIATI does to knowledge. A story built from the information in front of you will feel true, complete, and predictive, and it will be none of those things. The six chapters here are about what that feeling costs in business, medicine, forecasting, and the stock market. You did not know it all along Read the Google story and something happens. The pieces line up, the decisions connect, and the outcome arrives with a satisfying click. The feeling that you now understand what made Google succeed is the illusion. The test of a real explanation is whether it would have made the event predictable in advance. The Google story can't meet that test. No account of it can include the competing innovation that almost happened, the funding round that almost fell through, the market shift that could have arrived a year earlier. The mind is bad with nonevents, so the story is bad with them too. Luck plays a bigger role in the actual event than in the telling, and the more luck was involved, the less there is to learn. Hindsight bias makes this worse. Fischhoff and Beyth surveyed people before Nixon went to China and Russia in 1972 and asked them to assign probabilities to fifteen possible outcomes. Did Mao agree to meet? Did the US grant diplomatic recognition? Did the two superpowers agree on anything? After Nixon returned, the same people were asked what probabilities they had originally assigned. If the event happened, they remembered having been more confident about it. If it didn't happen, they remembered having thought it unlikely all along. The history of a belief gets rewritten the moment the belief changes, and you can't tell you're doing it. The consequences land hardest on people who make decisions for other people. Physicians, financial advisers, third-base coaches, CEOs, diplomats. It's easy to blame someone for a good decision that turned out badly, because the bad outcome makes the decision look obviously wrong. The Duluth flood case is the clean demonstration. Half the students saw only the information available when the city decided against hiring a bridge monitor. Twenty-four percent thought the city should have paid for the monitor. The other half was told that debris later blocked the river and caused major flooding. Fifty-six percent said the city should have hired the monitor, and that instruction not to let hindsight distort their judgment didn't touch it. The worse the consequence, the stronger the bias. The city had no way to know it would need a monitor, and now the monitor looks obviously necessary. The CEO is not the reason the company succeeded Every business book in the airport has the same promise. Take these leaders apart, find what they did, do the same thing. Kahneman runs the numbers and the promise falls apart. A generous estimate of the correlation between a firm's success and the quality of its CEO is about .30. To make that concrete, consider pairs of similar firms, where one has a stronger CEO. How often is the stronger CEO also running the more successful firm? Perfect predictability gives you 100% of pairs. Pure luck gives you 50%. A correlation of .30 gives you about 60%. The stronger CEO wins 10 percentage points more often than a coin toss, which is a real advantage, and it isn't the heroic figure the business press is selling. The Halo Effect, Philip Rosenzweig's book, names the mechanism. Business experts know whether a company has been doing well before they describe its CEO. A leader of a thriving firm gets called flexible, methodical, decisive. Let the same firm decline for a year and the same person becomes confused, rigid, authoritarian. Both descriptions feel correct at the time they're given. The causal direction gets reversed. The CEO doesn't make the firm rigid. The firm's trouble makes the CEO look rigid. Rosenzweig's conclusion is blunt, and it covers the whole genre. Stories of success and failure consistently overstate the impact of leadership and management practice, and their message is rarely useful. The track record backs him up. The firms in Built to Last were matched against less successful competitors, and the gap in profitability and stock returns shrank to almost nothing after the study. The companies from In Search of Excellence dropped sharply within a short time. Over a twenty-year period, Fortune's least-admired companies earned much higher stock returns than the most-admired ones. The average gap has to shrink, because part of the original gap was luck, and regression to the mean doesn't take requests. A compelling impression is not a forecast The term illusion of validity comes from Kahneman's own army service. Eight candidates, strangers to each other, insignia of rank removed, one obstacle field, one long log, and one wall about six feet high. The log could not touch the ground or the wall. He and a colleague took notes on who took charge, who tried to lead and got rebuffed, who berated a teammate after a failed attempt. Under the stress of the event, each man's true nature seemed to reveal itself. By the end of each run, they wrote their predictions with no doubt at all. Every few months came the feedback session. The army told them how the candidates had actually performed at officer school, and the predictions were barely better than blind guesses. The global evidence of past failure should have shaken their confidence, and it didn't. The next batch of candidates arrived the next morning, and the same certainty came back with them. Knowing the predictions were mostly useless as a general fact did nothing to the confidence felt in an individual case. The stock pickers cannot beat chance Kahneman visited a Wall Street firm in 1984 with Amos and Richard Thaler. He asked the senior investment manager the obvious question. When you sell a stock, who buys it? The manager waved at the window, meaning someone else very much like him. Both sides believe the other side is wrong about the price. Both sides can't be right. Terry Odean, a former student of Kahneman's, pulled seven years of trading records from 10,000 brokerage accounts, nearly 163,000 trades. He identified every instance where an investor sold one stock and soon bought another, which reveals a belief that the new stock will beat the old one. Over the year after the trade, the stocks people sold beat the stocks they bought by 3.2 percentage points, a gap that stands even after the costs of both trades. Taking a shower and doing nothing would have been the better policy. Mutual funds don't do better. At least two out of three underperform the market in any given year, and the year-to-year correlation between fund results is barely above zero. The funds that win in one year are mostly lucky. There is broad agreement among researchers that nearly all stock pickers are playing a game of chance, whether they know it or not, and very few of them know it. The cleanest evidence came from the wealth advisers. A firm of advisers to very wealthy clients gave Kahneman the eight-year results for twenty-five advisers. Each adviser's annual score determined their bonus. Kahneman ranked them by year and computed the correlation between every pair of years. Twenty-eight correlations. The average was .01. Zero. There was no persistent difference in skill to find. The executives who set the bonuses guessed "not very high" and weren't shocked when they heard the number. One of them drove Kahneman to the airport and said, with an edge, that he had done very well for the firm and no one could take that away. Kahneman thought about the morning's presentation and said nothing. That's the illusion of skill in one exchange. The finding threatens a livelihood and a self-image, so the mind files it where it will do no damage. Odean's later work with Barber added the demographic wrinkle. Men traded on their useless ideas more than women did, and as a result women earned better returns. The expert forecasters were beaten by random numbers Philip Tetlock ran the landmark study. He interviewed 284 people who made their living commenting on political and economic trends and collected more than 80,000 predictions. Would Gorbachev be ousted? Would the US go to war in the Persian Gulf? Each question had three outcomes, and the experts assigned probabilities to each. A person with no knowledge who assigned one-third to each outcome would have beaten the experts. Even in the regions they knew best, the specialists weren't significantly better than nonspecialists. The most knowledgeable forecasters were often the least reliable, because knowing more grows the confidence faster than it grows the accuracy. Tetlock writes that the point of diminishing returns for knowledge arrives disconcertingly quickly. The more famous the forecaster, the more flamboyant the forecasts, and TV producers love the confident ones. A hedgehog with one big theory makes better television than a fox who thinks everything depends on many interacting forces and a lot of luck. The foxes scored best and got invited to fewer shows. Tetlock reported that experts had an impressive collection of excuses when wrong. Off on timing. An unforeseeable event intervened. Wrong, but for the right reasons. The chapter's summary is two lines. Prediction errors are inevitable because the world is unpredictable, and high subjective confidence is not a reliable indicator of accuracy. The simple formula beat the trained professional Paul Meehl published a slim book in 1954 comparing two ways of predicting things. One used the trained judgment of a professional who had interviewed the person and reviewed the file. The other used a simple formula that combined a few scores by a fixed rule. Across twenty studies, the formula won. In the typical case, the counselors interviewed each student for forty-five minutes and also had high school grades, aptitude tests, and a four-page personal statement. The formula used high school grades and one aptitude test. It was more accurate than eleven of the fourteen counselors. The follow-up research runs about two hundred studies now, and the score has not changed. About 60% show significantly better accuracy for the algorithm, and most of the rest are ties. Since the algorithm is cheap, a tie counts as a win for the algorithm. This pattern shows up in the longevity of cancer patients, the length of hospital stays, credit risk, foster-parent suitability, recidivism, the winners of football games, and the future price of Bordeaux wine. Orley Ashenfelter, an economist and wine lover, built a formula for the future price of Bordeaux. Three inputs, the average summer temperature, the harvest rainfall, and the winter rainfall. The correlation between his predictions and the actual prices is above .90, and the formula beats the current prices of young wines. The reaction from the French wine trade, as The New York Times put it, ran somewhere between violent and hysterical. One expert called the findings ludicrous and absurd. Another said it was like judging movies without seeing them. Ashenfelter had built something that worked, and the people who tasted the wine for a living didn't want to hear it. Why does the formula win? Experts try to be clever. They consider combinations of features, and the complexity usually reduces accuracy rather than improving it. Humans are also inconsistent. Radiologists looking at the same chest X-ray on two occasions contradict themselves 20% of the time. A review of 41 studies of professional judgment found that level of inconsistency is typical. Unreliable judgments can't predict anything well, and the formula returns the same answer for the same input, every time. Robyn Dawes found that the exact weights don't even matter much. Assign equal weights to a set of valid predictors and you get close to the optimal formula, often better, because equal weights aren't affected by accidents in the original sample. His example was a formula for marital stability. Frequency of lovemaking minus frequency of quarrels. Don't let the result go negative. The best case for simple rules is the Apgar score. Until 1953, physicians and midwives used their own judgment to decide whether a newborn was in distress, and different practitioners watched different signs. Some checked breathing. Some watched for the cry. Danger signs were missed and infants died. Virginia Apgar wrote down five variables, heart rate, respiration, reflex, muscle tone, and color, each scored 0, 1, or 2, and rated infants one minute after birth. The score gave delivery rooms a consistent standard, and it's credited with a significant reduction in infant mortality. It's still used in every delivery room. The hostility to formulas has a moral flavor. Meehl collected the adjectives clinicians used for the statistical method. Mechanical, atomistic, dead, pedantic, sterile, blind. And for clinical judgment. Dynamic, holistic, subtle, deep, genuine, real. The cause of a mistake matters to people. A child dying because an algorithm erred is more poignant than the same death from human error, even when the algorithm makes fewer mistakes. Meehl's answer was that it's unethical to use intuition when a more accurate formula is available. Kahneman applied Meehl's argument to the Israeli army at twenty-one, when he was told to design a better interview for new recruits. He dropped the global impression the interviewer formed and had them score six specific traits one at a time, with factual questions for each, and kept the final combination for the formula. The interviewers nearly mutinied. One told him he was turning them into robots. He compromised and let them add one last thing after the scoring was done. Close your eyes, picture the recruit as a soldier, and give a number from 1 to 5. That compromise stuck with the system for decades. When the results came back, the sum of the six ratings predicted performance far better than the old interview had, and the "close your eyes" score did just as well as the sum. Intuition added real value, but only after the information had been collected and scored in a disciplined way. Kahneman gave the close-your-eyes number the same weight as the six traits combined. He visited the base forty-five years later and was told the interviews still worked well, and that they still finish with the line about closing your eyes. Intuition works only where the world repeats itself The obvious question is why anyone would trust a firefighter's sudden hunch after watching the stock pickers, the pundits, and the interviewers all fail at exactly that. Kahneman asked it too, and he spent years working it out with Gary Klein, whose entire career is about expert intuition in firefighters and nurses. Klein's fireground commanders don't compare options. They recognize a situation and one plan comes to mind. They simulate it mentally to check whether it will work, adjust if the simulation shows a shortcoming, and move on to the next idea only if the first one won't fix. Herbert Simon's definition is the honest one. The situation provides a cue. The cue gives the expert access to information stored in memory. The information provides the answer. Intuition is recognition. The kouros story from Gladwell's Blink is the same mechanism. Art experts looked at a marble statue that the Getty was about to buy and felt it was wrong, none of them able to say exactly why. One Italian art historian complained about the fingernails. A famous American expert's first thought was the word fresh. A Greek expert said anyone who had seen a sculpture come out of the ground could tell that thing had never been in the ground. The experts had the pattern. They didn't have the reason. For intuition to be skilled, two conditions have to hold. The environment has to be regular enough to be predictable, and the person has to have had a chance to learn its regularities. Chess is the extreme case. Ten thousand hours of dedicated practice is the usual estimate for reaching the top, which is about six years at five hours a day. Bridge and poker have enough regularity to support skill. Firefighters, nurses, and athletes face situations that are complex but orderly. The cues exist, and the people get feedback fast enough to learn them. Stock pickers and long-term political forecasters face the other kind of environment, which is zero-validity. There is no stable pattern to learn, so there is nothing for intuition to recognize, and the confident feeling is worth nothing. Klein and Kahneman ended with a rule that covers both worlds. Do not trust anyone, including yourself, to tell you how much to trust their judgment. Ask instead whether the environment is regular and whether the person had a chance to learn it. Some environments are worse than irregular. Robin Hogarth calls them wicked, meaning the professional learns the wrong lesson from experience. Hogarth borrows an example from Lewis Thomas. An early twentieth-century physician had intuitions about which patients would develop typhoid, and he tested each hunch by feeling the patient's tongue. He didn't wash his hands between patients. Patient after patient sickened, and his record got better and better. His predictions were accurate. They just had nothing to do with intuition, because he was the one spreading the disease. The boundary line isn't obvious from the inside. A psychotherapist is skilled at reading the moment in a session and has no skill at predicting how a patient will be doing next year. An anesthesiologist gets fast, clear feedback and develops useful hunches. A radiologist often doesn't learn how the diagnosis turned out, so the same kind of confidence never gets calibrated. An experienced professional who is skilled at some parts of her job has no reliable way to know which parts, and that gap between skill and the sense of skill is where overconfidence lives. The plan will take longer than the plan says The curriculum story is the one that embarrassed Kahneman for decades. He assembled a team to write a high-school textbook on judgment and decision making. Every Friday for a year, they worked on it. One afternoon, he asked everyone to write down how long they thought it would take to finish. The estimates clustered around two years, with a range from one and a half to two and a half. Then he asked Seymour Fox, the curriculum expert on the team, how long other teams had taken on similar projects. Fox thought for a moment and said about 40% of similar teams never finished at all, and the ones that did took seven to ten years. Asked to rank the team's own abilities against those other teams, Fox said below average, but not by much. That's the inside view versus the outside view. The inside view builds a forecast from the case in front of you, from your own plan and your own progress. It's WYSIATI applied to the future. The outside view ignores your case and looks at the class of similar cases, which is the only way to see the unknown unknowns you can't imagine on your own. The team should have quit that day. Nobody wanted to walk away from a project they had already spent a year on. They kept going. The book was finished eight years later, and by then the ministry had lost interest and nobody used it. That failure is the planning fallacy, and it's everywhere. The Scottish Parliament building was estimated at up to £40 million in 1997 and finished in 2004 at about £431 million. A study of rail projects from 1969 to 1998 found that passenger forecasts were overestimated in more than 90% of cases, by an average of 106%, with cost overruns of 45%. The forecasts didn't improve over thirty years of accumulating evidence. American homeowners remodeling kitchens expected to pay about $18,658 and paid $38,769 on average. Bent Flyvbjerg has spent decades on the fix, which is reference class forecasting. Find the class of similar projects, get the statistics of the class, and use those numbers as the baseline before adjusting for anything specific to your case. It works, and organizations still resist using it, because a realistic forecast is a harder sell than an optimistic one. One official told Flyvbjerg what a budget reserve becomes in the hands of contractors. Red meat to lions. The founder believes the odds do not apply Mild optimism is mostly a gift. Optimists are happier, more popular, more resilient, likelier to remarry, and probably live longer. The trouble starts when the optimism attaches to a specific risky plan. The stats are stark. About 35% of small businesses in the US survive five years. Entrepreneurs put the odds for a business like theirs at 60%, and their odds for their own venture much higher. Eighty-one percent put their personal chance of success at 7 in 10 or higher. Thirty-three percent said the chance of failing was zero. The Italian restaurant opening on the corner is not the story of someone who checked the odds and accepted them. The optimism shows up in how the odds are processed even when they're known. In Thomas Åstebro's study, a Canadian program gave inventors an objective assessment of their idea's commercial prospects, with grades D and E predicting failure. Only 5 of 411 projects in the lowest grade ever reached the market, and none succeeded. Even so, 47% of inventors kept working after being told the project was hopeless, and on average doubled their losses before quitting. Persistence after bad news was most common among inventors who scored highest on a personality measure of optimism. Kahneman's own example is a deserted motel on Vancouver Island, bought by a young couple who had been schoolteachers and used their life savings. They told him, without irony, that they had gotten it cheap because six or seven previous owners had failed at it. They didn't feel the need to explain why they would succeed where the others had not. They were also planning a loan to add a restaurant. Competition neglect is the cognitive piece. Colin Camerer and Dan Lovallo named it, and the chairman of Disney Studios gave the honest version. Asked why so many expensive films open on the same holiday weekends, he said hubris. If you only think about your own business, your own story department, your own marketing department, you don't think that everyone else is thinking the same way. There isn't enough audience to go around. The question that needs answering is how many people will see our film, considering what everyone else releases that weekend. The question the executives answer is whether they have a good film and a good marketing department, which is easier and more available. Kahneman's survey of startup founders makes the same point. Asked how much the outcome depends on what they do in their firm, the answers never came in under 80%. The number is surely wrong, because any startup's outcome depends as much on competitors and market shifts as on the founders' own efforts. The founders know their own plans best, and WYSIATI fills in the rest of the world with less detail, so their own actions look like almost the whole story. Overconfidence is socially rewarded The Duke survey asked chief financial officers of large corporations to predict the S&P 500's return for the following year. 11,600 forecasts. The correlation between their estimates and what actually happened was slightly below zero. When they said the market would fall, it was slightly more likely to rise. Then the survey asked for confidence intervals. Each CFO gave a number they were 90% sure would be too high and one they were 90% sure would be too low. The range between them is an 80% confidence interval, and if the intervals were honest, about 20% of outcomes should have fallen outside them. The actual rate of surprises was 67%. The range that would have produced the intended 20% surprise rate was more than four times wider, and it would have run from minus 10% to plus 30% every single year. No CFO would say that out loud. A wide range is a confession of ignorance, and the job description says knowledgeable. As Kahneman points out, Truman wanted a one-armed economist because he was tired of on-the-other-hand. Intensive care doctors show the same overconfidence in a setting where the stakes are as high as they get. A study compared autopsy findings with the diagnoses physicians gave while patients were alive, along with the physicians' stated confidence. Clinicians who were completely certain of the diagnosis were wrong 40% of the time. The social incentives reward the confidence, not the accuracy. Tetlock found the most overconfident experts got the most TV invitations. Medicine punishes visible uncertainty. A clinician who says out loud how little she knows about a case loses the patient's trust to the one who sounds sure. Kahneman and Lovallo coined a phrase for the pattern behind all of it. Bold forecasts and timid decisions. The risk takers aren't people with a bigger appetite for gambling. They're people who are less aware of the risks they're taking. The premortem gives doubt a job Gary Klein's premortem is the practical tool that came out of this part of the book. It runs at the moment a decision is almost final. Gather the people who know the decision, and give them this premise. Imagine we are a year into the future, we implemented the plan as it now exists, and the outcome was a disaster. Take five to ten minutes and write a brief history of that disaster. The method works for two reasons. It breaks the groupthink that sets in once a leader has tipped her hand and doubts get treated as disloyalty, and it gives permission to the people who do know the risks to say so. Kahneman describes mentioning it casually at Davos and hearing a CEO behind him mutter that it was worth coming for that alone. The other fixes from this part are less dramatic. Take the outside view on any long project and find the reference class before trusting your own progress. Run a hiring or admissions process by collecting information on one trait at a time and scoring each before moving on, then decide by the total rather than by the interview impression. When a professional with real expertise in one area makes a confident prediction outside it, ask the two questions from the Klein collaboration. Is the environment regular, and did this person have a chance to learn it? Some experts do beat the odds One Part 3 result has since grown a second half. Tetlock didn't stop at the 2005 book. He ran forecasting tournaments for the intelligence community, and a small group of predictors stayed accurate two years running. The superforecasters were trained, they thought in probabilities instead of slogans, they updated on small pieces of news, and they stayed fox-like. The average pundit's record didn't improve. The best forecasters are real, rare, and made rather than found. Tetlock's 2005 verdict holds, with an exception carved out. Everything else in this part has held up. Hindsight bias survived three decades of retests, showing up in what people remember, what they think was likely, and how they rate their own predictions. The clinical-versus-mechanical question got its meta-analysis, and the algorithm came out about 10% more accurate on average, with a clear mechanical win in 33% to 47% of studies and a clear human win in only 6% to 16%. The Duke CFO survey got a successor with a decade of newer data, and the executives came out just as miscalibrated. The 10,000-hour number is the one that took real damage. A meta-analysis of deliberate practice across fields found it explains about a quarter of the variance in games, a fifth in music, and less than 1% in professions. The two conditions for skilled intuition are untouched. The tidy number attached to them is not. Part 4 moves to the choices themselves. Prospect theory, loss aversion, the endowment effect, and the fourfold pattern, which is where Kahneman and Tversky finally built the alternative to the rational model they had spent a decade tearing down. Practical takeaways Ask whether a forecast would have been possible before the event, not after. If only hindsight makes it look obvious, it was never obvious. Find the reference class before I trust the inside view. How did similar projects or companies actually turn out? Keep a written record of my predictions and the reasoning behind them, so the later me can't quietly edit what the earlier me believed. When a leader looks brilliant, check the company's numbers first. Halo effects run backward from outcomes to traits. Treat confident stock tips, market forecasts, and pundit predictions as entertainment. The base rates say nobody beats the market reliably. Don't trust someone's confidence as a measure of their accuracy. Ask about the environment and their learning history instead. When a decision is nearly final, run a premortem. Imagine it's a year later and the plan failed, and write the history of why. Before a big project, look up how long similar projects took for other people. Then believe that number over my own estimate. References The load-bearing studies from Part 3, sorted by theme. items.content_text: Thinking, Fast and Slow, Part 2. Heuristics and Biases A phone poll of 300 seniors says 60% support the president. Summarize it in three words and you say "elderly support president." Nobody says "300-person poll." The sample size almost never makes it into the story. The missing sample size is the whole of Part 2. System 1 is excellent at stories and hopeless at statistics, and the nine chapters here are nine demonstrations of it. Anchors, availability, base rates, the hot hand, the Linda problem. Part 1 covered how the mind works. This part covers what it does to numbers. Rural counties are both the sickest and the healthiest A study of all 3,141 US counties found that the lowest kidney cancer rates were in rural, sparsely populated, Republican counties in the Midwest, the South, and the West. Clean country living, said the obvious story. Then the counties with the highest rates turned out to be rural, sparsely populated, and in the same states. Poverty, bad medical care, high-fat diet, said the other obvious story. Both stories were built in seconds. Only one of them can be true. The real answer is that rural counties are small, and small samples are extreme. Kahneman's version of the demo is a marble urn. Draw four marbles from a half-red, half-white urn and all four come out the same color far more often than you expect. Jack's four-marble samples produce homogeneous draws about 12.5% of the time. Jill's seven-marble samples do it 1.56% of the time. A factor of eight, and neither of them did anything to the urn. Kahneman and Tversky's first joint paper was about this, and its title was a joke. They called it "Belief in the Law of Small Numbers," by which they meant the conviction that the law of large numbers applies to small numbers too. The paper's most quoted line is a recommendation that researchers treat their statistical intuitions "with proper suspicion and replace impression formation by computation whenever possible." The line existed because they had caught themselves. Kahneman had been choosing samples so small that his own experiments had a 50% chance of missing a true effect, and he taught statistics. When they tested the Society of Mathematical Psychology, including authors of two statistics textbooks, every error Kahneman had made showed up in a large majority of the respondents. The experts were no better. Schools got the same treatment. The Gates Foundation noticed that the best-performing schools in Pennsylvania were disproportionately small, and put $1.7 billion into creating and splitting small schools. The worst-performing schools were also disproportionately small, which nobody had checked. Small schools are not better. They are more variable. In higher grades, large schools do better, because a big school can offer more courses. The hot hand is the same illusion applied to sports. Gilovich, Vallone, and Tversky looked at thousands of shots from the Philadelphia 76ers and found no streakiness in field goals or free throws. The sequence of makes and misses satisfies every test of randomness. Players, coaches, and fans are certain the effect is real. Red Auerbach's response to the study is a compact summary of how the finding landed. "Who is this guy? So he makes a study. I couldn't care less." Kahneman's own version of the story is from the Yom Kippur War. Two Israeli squadrons flew from the same base. One lost four planes, the other lost none. An inquiry opened to find what the unlucky squadron was doing wrong. Kahneman told the air force to stop. There was no prior reason to expect a difference, and the search would have attached blame to men who had already lost friends. Any number in front of you is doing something Kahneman and Tversky built a wheel of fortune that could only stop on 10 or 65. Students watched it spin, wrote down the number, and then estimated the percentage of African nations in the UN. The students who saw 10 guessed 25% on average. The students who saw 65 guessed 45%. A wheel of fortune cannot contain information about the UN, and it moved the answers anyway. That is anchoring. The effect is not small and it is not fragile. Visitors at the Exploratorium estimated the height of the tallest redwood. The two groups got anchors of 1,200 feet and 180 feet, and produced estimates of 844 and 282 feet. The anchors were 1,020 feet apart. The answers came out 562 feet apart, giving Kahneman's anchoring index, which is that ratio, a value of 55%. Random anchors score as high as plausible ones. You do not have to believe the number for it to work. The demonstrations get uncomfortable. German judges with an average of fifteen years on the bench read a shoplifting case and rolled a pair of dice loaded to come up 3 or 9. Then they set a sentence. The judges who rolled 9 gave 8 months on average. The judges who rolled 3 gave 5. A different study found real estate agents valuing an actual house were moved 41% of the way by an asking price they later denied using. The students with no real estate experience were more anchored still, and at least admitted it. Kahneman spent decades arguing with Tversky about whether anchoring was deliberate adjustment or suggestion. They never settled it. The answer, found after Tversky's death, is that they were both right. There are two mechanisms, one per system. System 2 adjusts from the anchor and stops too early. System 1 does something closer to priming, quietly activating everything that fits the number. Mussweiler and Strack showed the priming version by anchoring the temperature in Germany at 20°C or 5°C, then testing word recognition. The warm anchor made summer words like sun and beach easier to recognize. The cold one made frost and ski easier. The numbers had changed what the subjects could see. The defense that works is to think the opposite. Galinsky and Mussweiler had negotiators argue against the anchor. The effect shrank. An instruction to consider the minimal offer the other side would accept did it too. For an outrageous opening offer, Kahneman's advice was not a matching outrageous counter. Make a scene, threaten to walk, and refuse to negotiate from that number. Easy to recall is not the same as common WWhich pair of letters can make more words, XUZONLCJM or TAPCERHOB? You knew almost instantly, and you did not generate a single word. The availability heuristic is the mind substituting ease of retrieval for frequency. It never counts. It feels. Substituting ease of recall for frequency is why the news distorts what you fear. Slovic, Lichtenstein, and Fischhoff asked people to compare causes of death, and the pattern is consistent. Strokes kill about twice as many people as all accidents combined, and 80% of respondents judged accidents more likely. Tornadoes were rated as deadlier than asthma, which kills 20 times as many people. Death by lightning is 52 times more common than death by botulism, and people put it the other way around. Media coverage is biased toward novelty and poignancy, and the mind reads vivid as frequent. The marriage version is one of the few findings here with a practical fix. Ross and Sicoly asked spouses what percentage of the housework they did. The two answers summed to well over 100%. Each partner remembers their own effort and not the other's, and the difference in memory becomes a difference in perceived fairness. The same thing happens on any team. Everyone feels like they did more than their share, because everyone's own work is available and everyone else's is not. Kahneman says this is one of the few biases you can talk yourself out of. There is more than 100% of the credit to go around, and everyone in the room is feeling the same thing. Then Schwarz's German group found the twist. Ask people to list six times they behaved assertively, and they rate themselves assertive. Ask for twelve and the rating drops, even though twelve is more evidence. Fluency is doing the work. The first three or four instances come easily and the last few are a struggle, and the struggle gets read as a verdict. People asked for twelve instances of meek behavior rated themselves as quite assertive, because they could not easily come up with examples of meekness. The effect flips when the person cares. Students with a family history of heart disease stopped going by ease and started going by content. If they managed to list many risky behaviors, they felt at risk. If they came up with many safe ones, they felt safe. A loaded System 2 uses the number of instances. A comfortable one uses the feeling. A minor scare can reset a government's priorities Ask people to rate technologies for benefits and risks, and the two ratings come out inversely correlated. Things people like have large benefits and small risks. Things they dislike have small benefits and large risks. Nobody in the study was weighing tradeoffs. One feeling was answering both questions at once. Slovic calls this the affect heuristic. Members of the British Toxicology Society showed the same pattern. Expertise did not protect them. Kuran and Sunstein named the way private worry turns into public policy. They called it the availability cascade. A minor story gets covered. Some of the public gets worried, which is itself a story, which produces more coverage. Worry builds until no politician can ignore it, and the issue resets the priorities of an entire government. Two cases in the book, both contested to this day. Love Canal is the first. Buried toxic waste surfaced after heavy rain in 1979, and the residents were furious and frightened. Coverage went daily, ABC News aired a special, and empty baby-size coffins were carried in front of the legislature. A resident named Lois Gibbs kept the story alive through the worst of it. The law that followed, CERCLA, created the Superfund and is a real achievement of environmental legislation. It was also expensive, and claims of actual health damage were never substantiated. Kahneman reports both facts and lets you sit with them. The Alar scare is the second. A chemical sprayed on apples to improve their appearance was linked to tumors in rodents at enormous doses. Meryl Streep testified before Congress. The apple industry took large losses, and one citizen called a phone-in to ask whether it was safer to pour apple juice down the drain or take it to a toxic waste dump. The FDA banned the chemical. Later research found a possible very small risk. The net effect on public health was probably negative, because people ate fewer apples. The shape underneath is probability neglect. We ignore small risks or we panic about them, and there is nothing in between. Every parent waiting up for a teenager will recognize it. You know the odds are fine and the images of disaster come anyway. Slovic's line for it is that you are imagining the numerator, the one tragic story from the news, and never thinking about the denominator. Terrorism runs on the same mechanism on purpose. The casualty count next to traffic deaths is small. The images repeat forever, and fear does not do arithmetic. A personality sketch beats enrollment data, every time Rank nine graduate fields by how likely Tom W is to be in each one. With no other information, you use enrollment numbers, which is correct. Give people a personality sketch first, and things change. Tom W was written to be brilliant but uncreative, orderly, fond of corny sci-fi puns, and short on sympathy for other people. It was designed to fit engineering and computer science, which are small fields, and to fit the huge fields of humanities and social work badly. It worked exactly as designed. Kahneman wrote it in the early morning hours, showed it to a statistician colleague named Robyn Dawes, and watched him guess "computer scientist?" Dawes caught his own mistake the moment Kahneman said "base rate," but he had not thought of it on his own. If the statistician could not see the base rate past the sketch, nobody was going to. The Tom W description is not even trustworthy. The instructions said it was based on tests of uncertain validity. Nobody cared. WYSIATI, from Part 1, is at work. The story is available, the source is not, and the mind builds the best case it can from whatever is in front of it. Kahneman's advice is to keep probability judgments close to the base rate when the evidence is weak, and he is blunt that this takes real self-control. The cab problem makes base rates vivid. A city has 85% green cabs and 15% blue cabs. A witness says the hit-and-run cab was blue, and the witness gets color right 80% of the time. The correct answer is 41%, not the 80% most people give, because the base rate is doing real work. Now change one thing. Say the two companies have equal fleets, and green cabs cause 85% of accidents. Same math, and this time people use it. The second version gets used, because it has a cause in it. Reckless green drivers, and now the base rate attaches to individual drivers the way a trait does. Kahneman is careful here. He calls stereotyping neutral in the psychological sense and points out that reliance on causal base rates is exactly what improved accuracy in the cab problem. The social norm against stereotyping exists for good reasons, and he agrees with the norm. His point is narrower. The norm has costs, and pretending it does not is not honest. The Nisbett and Borgida study should end every argument about teaching psychology. Students learned about a study where participants talked over intercoms and one had a seizure. Only 4 of the 15 helped right away. The students read the results, watched bland videos of two actual participants, and predicted the two men would rush to help. Their predictions matched students who had never seen the results at all. Then Borgida showed a different group the videos and simply said the two men had not helped. Those students immediately guessed the group numbers correctly. The detailed story always feels more likely than the plain one Linda is thirty-one, single, outspoken, and very bright. She majored in philosophy, cared about discrimination and social justice, and went to antinuclear demonstrations. Which is more probable, that Linda is a bank teller, or that Linda is a bank teller active in the feminist movement? Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller, so the second option can only be less probable. In Kahneman and Tversky's studies, 85% to 90% of undergraduates picked it anyway. So did 85% of Stanford decision science PhD students, who had taken multiple courses in probability. When Kahneman asked a large class whether they realized they had violated an elementary logical rule, someone in the back row shouted "So what?" One student explained herself by saying she thought she had only been asked for her opinion. Stephen Jay Gould knew the right answer and wrote that a little homunculus in his head kept shouting that she could not just be a bank teller. The dinnerware version of the same structure is Hsee's, and it is worth reading slowly. Set A has 40 pieces, including some broken ones. Set B has 24 pieces, all intact. Compare them side by side and people pay more for A, correctly, because A contains everything in B plus extra good dishes. Show only one set to each person and B wins at $33 against $23. Less is more. The mind averages the set instead of adding it up, and System 1's averaging also explains why the detailed Linda story beats the plain one. The fix that came out of the research is almost comically small. One health survey asked "what percentage of the men are over 55 and have had a heart attack" and produced 65% errors. Another wording asked "how many of the 100 participants are over 55 and have had a heart attack," and errors fell to 25%. A count of 100 people brings up actual people you can sort into corners of a room, and once you can see the groups, containment is obvious. Percentages stay abstract, and abstract numbers do not show you that one group sits inside another. Kahneman's takeaway from the Linda saga is not about the fallacy. It is about the fight. The problem drew years of criticism, and the criticism zeroed in on the weakest part of the case while the stronger between-subjects findings went unaddressed. He compares it to the two styles of courtroom attack and says the social sciences allow the political style of argument when large issues are at stake. The prevalence of bias in human judgment is a large issue. A cadet's best day is mostly luck, and so is his worst Flight instructors in the Israeli Air Force told Kahneman he was wrong about praise. They praised a cadet after a clean maneuver and he did worse next time. They screamed after a bad one and he improved. Punishment worked, reward did not, and they had the data to prove it. They had misread regression to the mean. Praise goes to the unusually good attempt, and the unusually good attempt is partly luck. The next attempt is more ordinary because the luck has reset, not because the praise hurt. The bad attempts were unusually bad and improved on their own. Kahneman's demo for the instructors was to have every officer throw two coins at a target with his back turned. Score the first throws from best to worst and the pattern appears on the blackboard. The best first throws got worse. The worst got better. No praise, no punishment. He called the instructors' situation an unfortunate contingency of the human condition. Because we are nice when people do well and harsh when they do badly, life punishes us for being nice and rewards us for being harsh. The feedback is perverse, and it is the default. Talent and luck both shape the outcome, so the extreme results are the ones where luck went far from average. That is why the golfer who shoots 66 on day one is expected to come back toward the field on day two. It is also the whole of the Sports Illustrated jinx, which needs no jinx at all. The cover goes to a player who had an extraordinary season, which almost certainly included a luck streak, and luck does not persist. Kahneman's own example is the Olympic ski jump he watched while writing a paper with Amos. Each athlete got two jumps. The sportscaster explained that Norway's good first jump would leave him tense and protective of the lead, while Sweden's bad one would free him up. The second jump regresses either way, and the story explained nothing. Francis Galton discovered the effect in the 1880s and needed years and the help of the best statisticians of his era to understand it. The party version Kahneman gives is worth keeping. "Highly intelligent women tend to marry men who are less intelligent than they are" is interesting and provocative and gets people arguing about mate selection. "The correlation between spouses' intelligence is less than perfect" is obvious and boring. The two statements are algebraically identical. The interesting one is the boring one said a different way. The depressed children headline is the practical version. Treat a group of depressed kids with an energy drink for three months and they improve. So would kids who hug a cat for twenty minutes a day, or stand on their heads, because depressed children are an extreme group and extreme groups move back toward the middle on their own. That is what a control group is for. Without one, you are mostly measuring time. Your best forecast is more boring than your best judgment Julie read fluently at age four. Predict her college GPA. The intuitive answer lands around 3.7 or 3.8, because early reading gets translated to the top of the scale with no discount applied. The trouble is that early reading and college GPA only share some causes. Kahneman's estimate is that they share about 30%. The correction has four steps, and they apply to any numeric prediction. Start with the average GPA, which is what you would guess if you knew nothing about Julie. Then find the GPA that matches your impression of the evidence, which is the intuitive answer. Then estimate the correlation between your evidence and the outcome. Then move only that fraction of the distance from the average toward your intuition. With a correlation of .30, you get 30% of the way there, and a number that feels too boring to be useful. The military version shows what happens without the correction. Officers at an IDF selection unit rated candidates and were also asked to predict each candidate's final grade at officer school. The distribution of the predictions was almost identical to the distribution of the officers' own ratings. They had not predicted anything. They had translated their existing impression onto a new scale and skipped the uncertainty entirely. The cost of correcting is psychological, and Kahneman is honest about it. An unbiased prediction never calls the extreme case. A venture capitalist who forecasts honestly will never get to say "this is the next Google" about a company in its early days, because almost nothing that early deserves that certainty. She will also miss some real winners, and that is a real loss. The procedure is worth the effort when the stakes are high, and the effort is real. The hiring version is the one to take to work. Kim just finished grad school with spectacular recommendations and a brilliant talk, and she has no track record. Jane has three excellent postdoc years with a less sparkly interview. The intuitive pick is Kim, because the impression is stronger, and stronger is not the same as more informative. Jane's file is a larger sample. Kim's is smaller, so it's more likely to contain extremes that will not repeat. Kahneman says he would vote for Jane, and that it would be a struggle to override his own impression. The hot hand came back One Part 2 result has since been revised, and it is the one everybody remembers. Miller and Sanjurjo reanalyzed the original 76ers data in 2018 and found a bias in how the streak percentages were measured. Correct the bias and the same data shows evidence of streak shooting, which the 1985 paper had ruled out. Later work has kept the effect small and mostly limited to near-identical shots, like free throws and three-point contests, and the in-game evidence is still mixed. Everything else in these chapters has held up better. Anchoring has replicated across dozens of settings, including a large multi-lab project that reran the Jacowitz and Kahneman estimation-task version and found the effect even larger than the original study did. Availability effects, base-rate neglect, the conjunction fallacy, and regression to the mean have all survived their retests. The hot hand is the one to stop quoting. Part 3 goes after confidence itself. Overconfidence, the illusion that we understand the past, the illusion that we can see the future, and why experts are so sure about things they are about to get wrong. The narrative fallacy comes first, and it is where every clean success story falls apart. Practical takeaways Check the sample before I believe the pattern. Small samples produce extremes, and next year it will be different counties. Treat every number on the table as live. The first offer in a negotiation is already inside my estimate. Ask what the news is not showing me. Availability is built from coverage, and coverage is built on novelty. When a panic arrives, do the denominator math before I move any of my money or my opinions. Write down the base rate before I let a personality sketch or a vivid story move it. Run the regression correction on any numeric forecast. Average first, intuition second, then move only the correlation's share of the distance. Notice when I am being nice or nasty to someone. The feedback I get back is systematically misleading, and knowing that is most of the fix. References The load-bearing studies from Part 2, sorted by theme. items.content_text: Thinking, Fast and Slow, Part 1. Two Systems A bat and a ball cost $1.10 between them. The bat costs a dollar more than the ball. How much does the ball cost? Ten cents arrives on its own. Wrong, of course. The ball costs five cents, and the correct answer takes a moment of real arithmetic. Kahneman opens with a failure that small because it shows how the mind gets from question to answer. One process throws an answer at you without being asked. Another checks it, when it bothers. He calls them System 1 and System 2, and he keeps reminding you that they are fiction. There is no one part of the brain where either one lives. A sentence about a character is easier to think with than a sentence about a computation, and he wants you thinking with these two characters for the rest of the book. This is the first post in a series on the book. Part 1 covers the two systems themselves, attention and effort, self-control, priming, cognitive ease, our habit of seeing causes, and how the mind jumps to conclusions. It's the foundation for everything that follows. You can be blind to the obvious and to your own blindness System 1 orients you to a sudden sound and finishes "bread and butter" before you decide to. It reads billboards, spots hostility in a voice, knows that 2 + 2 is 4. System 2 does the rest. Multiplication problems, tax forms, narrow parking spaces. It's slow, serial, expensive, and it spends a budget of attention that can't be spent twice. The gorilla study settles the argument about that budget. Viewers count passes by the white team and ignore the black team. Halfway through, a woman in a gorilla suit crosses the court, thumps her chest, and leaves. She's on screen for nine seconds. About half of viewers never see her, and the ones who miss her are certain she was never there. Kahneman's summary is blunt. We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness. Vision makes the same point in miniature. The two lines in the Müller-Lyer display stay unequal forever. You can measure them, accept the numbers, and still see one as longer. The belief updates. The perception refuses. He tells a matching story from his graduate training about the charming patient with a history of failed therapy, the one who makes every new clinician feel uniquely equipped to save him. That feeling is the warning sign. Learn the pattern, refuse to act on it, and go on feeling it anyway. There's no off switch. Show a reader a word in a language they know and they read it, unless their attention is somewhere else entirely. Nobody can hide how hard they are thinking Kahneman spent a year in a hypnosis lab early in his career, and the research topic he settled on there was the pupil of the eye. He had read Eckhard Hess on the pupil as a window to the soul, and he and Jackson Beatty built a chin rest, camera, and metronome setup to photograph dilation during paced mental work. The task was Add-1. Four digits arrive on metronome beats, two beats pass, and you say each digit plus one while keeping the rhythm. Add-3 is the brutal version, the most demanding task Kahneman ever measured. The body cooperates with the measurement. During Add-3 the pupil swells by roughly half its area and the heart speeds up by about seven beats a minute. The effort curve climbs to a peak, holds, then relaxes as the digits leave memory. Beatty and Kahneman projected the pupil on a screen in the corridor and learned to tell when a subject had given up. They would ask why the work had stopped. The answer was usually a startled "how did you know?" followed by the line about the window to the soul. Casual conversation, they noticed, left the pupil small. Mental life normally runs at walking pace inside a comfortable rhythm, and sprints are rare. Under a real sprint, people go blind. Subjects watching for a flashing letter during Add-1 caught it almost every time at the start and near the end of the task, and missed it nearly half the time when the load peaked, with their wide-open eyes pointed straight at it. Effort is a cost, so people take the cheapest route that works. Skill lowers the cost. Switching tasks raises it. The most demanding slow thinking is the kind that forces you to think fast. Your willpower runs low and sugar brings it back Self-control and hard thinking pull from the same supply. Load people with seven digits and they choose chocolate cake over fruit salad more often, make more selfish choices, and settle for superficial judgments. A few drinks and a bad night's sleep do the same damage. Roy Baumeister's lab showed the pattern across tasks. Stifling your feelings during a sad film weakens your grip on a hand dynamometer later. Eating radishes while the cookies sit there makes you quit a hard puzzle sooner. The strangest result is the glucose one. Effortful thinking measurably lowers blood sugar, and a glass of lemonade with real sugar brings the depleted performance back. The same lemonade sweetened with Splenda does not. This is less tidy than it sounds, and the ego depletion finding has not held up well since. The parole study is the one that sticks. Eight Israeli judges reviewed parole applications for six minutes apiece, denied by default, and approved about 35% overall. Right after a food break, the approval rate jumped to about 65%. Two hours later, it was near zero. The parole numbers are grim, and they should be read grimly. Bad decisions are usually not character flaws. They're what an exhausted, hungry system produces. Harvard students get the bat and ball wrong too More than half of the Harvard, MIT, and Princeton students who saw the bat-and-ball problem answered with the intuitive ten cents. At less selective universities, the failure rate passed 80%. The flowers syllogism fooled a majority too. All roses are flowers, some flowers fade quickly, so some roses fade quickly, except the conclusion doesn't follow, and the pull of "true, true" makes it hard to check. Shane Frederick built the Cognitive Reflection Test out of three of these puzzles, and the low scorers aren't short on intelligence. They're short on the willingness to check an answer that felt fine. Sixty-three percent of the intuitive responders would take $3,400 this month over $3,800 next month, against 37% of the careful ones. In Walter Mischel's cookie test, four-year-olds who waited fifteen minutes for the second cookie later scored higher on intelligence tests, and the link ran through attention control. Keith Stanovich spent decades on this question and concluded that rationality and intelligence are separate abilities. A high IQ buys you no protection against lazy thinking. Words you never noticed are steering your behavior Read the words bananas and vomit next to each other and your body reacts before you have an opinion. The face twists, the heart rate ticks up, the mind invents a quick story in which bananas caused the sickness, and a set of related ideas becomes easier to reach for a while. One idea activates many others, most of them silently, and only a few reach consciousness. Priming is where this gets strange. Show people the word EAT and the fragment SO_P becomes SOUP more often than SOAP. Bargh's students assembled scrambled sentences sprinkled with elderly words, walked to the next experiment, and walked it more slowly. A German study got the effect in reverse, with slow walking making old-age words come easier. Nodding through an editorial made students agree with it. Shaking made them disagree. A polling station in a school nudged votes toward school funding. Reminders of money made people more independent, more selfish, and willing to sit 118 centimeters from a stranger instead of 80. The honesty box at a British office fits here. One week the sign above the price list showed a pair of eyes, and the next it showed flowers, with no comment from anyone. On eye weeks, contributions ran nearly three times higher than on flower weeks. Nobody believed the poster was watching. Nobody had to. Also, a fair amount of this research has crumbled since 2011. Hold that thought. Clear fonts make lies feel true Cognitive ease has one signal and a crowd of causes. A clean font, a repeated sentence, a good mood, and an easy rhyme all push a message toward feeling easy, and easy carries a feeling that the thing in front of you is true and familiar. The feeling doesn't carry a source label. Larry Jacoby showed that people will mistake a made-up name for a celebrity name days after seeing it once, purely because it reads more fluently the second time. Repetition alone can install a fact. People who saw the phrase "the body temperature of a chicken" several times accepted a statement that the temperature is 144 degrees, a number they had never been told. "Adolf Hitler was born in 1892" beats "Adolf Hitler was born in 1887," and both are false. Rhyming aphorisms get rated as more insightful than the same claims without the rhyme. Stock reports from a broker named Artan get more weight than reports from a broker named Taahhut, because one name is easier to say, and effort is aversive. Then the result that flips the intuition. Princeton students took the Cognitive Reflection Test in either a clean font or a washed-out gray one. The strained group made at least one mistake 35% of the time. The comfortable group did 90% of the time. A hard-to-read page wakes System 2 up, and the wakeful system catches more of the shortcuts. Ease, meanwhile, builds affection. Zajonc's Turkish words, printed in college newspapers at different frequencies, got rated more favorably the more often readers had seen them, and chicks exposed to a tone before hatching complained less when they heard it after. Mood works the same way. In the remote associates test, happy subjects more than doubled their accuracy on linked triads like dive, light, rocket, and unhappy subjects performed at chance. Your brain invents causes before the sentence ends Fred's parents arrived late. The caterers were expected soon. Fred was angry. Your mind assigns the cause instantly. It isn't the caterers. Ask how many animals of each kind Moses took onto the ark, and a surprising number miss the problem. Sentences with a wrong word in the middle, like Earth revolves around the trouble every year, trigger a distinct brain response within two-tenths of a second. A male voice saying "I believe I am pregnant" lands wrong just as fast. Kahneman's own case is a psychologist he kept meeting on his travels, once on a tiny island resort and once in a London theater after the lights went down. The second meeting was statistically less likely than the first, and he was less surprised by it, because the first one had already made running into Jon feel normal. Michotte showed that people see physical causation the way they see color. Six-month-olds register surprise when the sequence of one object launching another gets altered. Heider and Simmel's film of two triangles and a circle runs a minute and forty seconds, and almost every viewer reports a chase, a bullying, a rescue, and a violent ending. The perception of intention is impossible to resist, and only people afflicted by autism do not experience it. The problem is where that instinct lands. Statistics asks you to draw conclusions about categories from properties of the group, and System 1 can't do that. So the causal story wins by default, and the story is often wrong. On the day Saddam Hussein was captured, Bloomberg reported that treasuries rose because the capture might not curb terrorism, then reported that they fell because the capture boosted risky assets. The same event explained both directions. A statement that explains everything explains nothing, and it still felt like news. Confidence comes from the story, not from the evidence Ask whether Mindik will be a good leader, and offer two adjectives, intelligent and strong. The answer comes back yes, immediately. The next sentence adds corrupt and cruel, and the first judgment looks foolish. Kahneman's name for this is WYSIATI. What you see is all there is. Associative memory builds the best story it can from the pieces in front of it, and it can't account for the pieces that never arrived. One-sided evidence makes people more confident, not less. Participants in a study of a labor dispute read either one lawyer's brief or both, and the ones who heard a single side ended up more sure of their verdicts, even though they knew the setup and could have written the other argument themselves. Confidence tracks the coherence of the story, not its completeness. The halo effect runs the same way. Meet Joan at a party, like her, and later rate her as generous when nobody has observed a generous act. Solomon Asch showed that the identical six adjectives produce a better person in the order intelligent, industrious, impulsive, critical, stubborn, envious than in the reverse order. First impressions rewrite the meaning of everything that follows them. Kahneman's own grading story belongs here. For years he read each student's exam booklet straight through and graded as he went, then noticed his scores within a booklet were suspiciously alike. He switched to grading one question across every student before moving to the next, the scores spread out, and his confidence fell. The confidence was the illusion. The same lesson scales up to meetings. Judgments made in a group after open discussion are correlated judgments, and averaging correlated errors does not cancel them out. Write the positions down first, then talk. Todorov's faces make the point uncomfortable. Princeton students rated campaign portraits for competence after a tenth of a second of exposure, and those ratings picked the winner in about 70% of senate, house, and governor races. The skill came from reading faces for dominance and trustworthiness, and television gave it a bigger role. For low-information voters who watch a lot of TV, the face effect ran about three times larger. The old reflex votes. Your mood answers questions you were never asked The mind rarely gets stuck. Ask a hard question like how happy you are with your life, and System 1 quietly swaps in an easier one, like what mood you're in right now, and hands back an answer. Kahneman calls the swap substitution, and the answer feels like an answer to the question you asked. The illusion in the corridor of the three men works the same way. The figure on the right looks taller because the drawing is in perspective, so the eye answers a question about height in a three-dimensional scene instead of size on the page, and the answer overwhelms the actual question that was asked. The dating survey is the cleanest example in the book. Students asked about happiness and then asked about dates showed no connection between the two answers. Students asked about dates first showed a correlation of .66 between dates and happiness. Nothing about their lives had changed. A mood had been installed, and it answered the next question for them. Paul Slovic's affect heuristic is the same shortcut applied to beliefs. If you like the current health policy, its benefits look substantial and its costs manageable. Dislike nuclear power and its risks look high and its benefits small. Change the risk rating alone and the benefits rating follows. That shouldn't happen if you were weighing evidence. System 2, in this mode, is more an apologist for the emotions of System 1 than a critic of them. Kahneman says most of this runs silently. System 1 shapes many of your choices and judgments, and you never see it working. Some of this science has not held up The social priming chapter has aged worst. The Florida effect failed a careful replication, and the money priming results have had a rough record in replication attempts. Kahneman himself has written about the field's trouble reproducing some of these findings. Ego depletion is the other casualty. A large preregistered multi-lab effort found an effect near zero, which makes the lemonade story thinner than the book's confidence suggests. The parole study picked up a serious objection too. The case order wasn't random. Prisoners with lawyers were heard earlier, and unrepresented prisoners later, which can produce the same downward slide without any glucose story at all. The core still stands. The bat-and-ball result is one of the most reliable findings in the field. The gorilla replicates. Truth by repetition replicates. WYSIATI and substitution describe something real, and the two-system sketch in this part is still the best entry point to the literature. The book's most famous demonstrations are more fragile than the book lets on, and that's worth knowing before you quote the parole study at a dinner party. Part 2 picks up where this leaves off, with the heuristics themselves. Anchors, availability, the law of small numbers, Linda the bank teller, and the long-running puzzle of why statistics is so hard for a mind built for stories. Practical takeaways Write my judgment down before the meeting starts, not after the loudest person has spoken. Do the hardest thinking early. By evening, the easy answer wins by default. Ask what's missing before trusting how confident the story makes me feel. Treat fluency as a warning, not a signal. A clear font and a repeated sentence are not evidence. Slow down when the question is unfamiliar and the stakes are high. Check the easy answer. Ten cents felt fine for a reason, and the reason was not truth. items.content_text: Can machines ever be moral agents? That’s the question I’ve been chewing on lately, especially as AI keeps showing up in more high-stakes places. Not “can AI do good things” or “can it follow rules”, but the deeper one, can it actually own moral responsibility the way a person does? Spoiler: I’m skeptical. Here’s why, through the usual ethical lenses, and how it plays out with real-world messes. Kant: Duty, Reason, and the Problem of Intention Kant’s big idea is that moral worth comes from acting out of duty, guided by pure practical reason. You don’t just do the right thing because it feels good or produces nice results, you do it because the categorical imperative says so. Treat people as ends, not means. Act only on maxims you’d will as universal law. AI can spit out answers that look Kantian. It can refuse to help with certain requests, cite principles, even generate long arguments about dignity. But there’s no will behind it. No capacity to legislate moral law for itself. No genuine respect for the moral law. It’s pattern-matching and optimization under constraints set by humans. If an autonomous weapon system “decides” not to fire because of some programmed rule about civilian harm, that isn’t the machine acting from duty. It’s executing code. The moral responsibility stays with the people who wrote the rules, approved the deployment, and chose to put a machine in that loop. Kant would say the machine lacks the rational autonomy required for true moral agency. Utilitarianism: Counting Consequences Is Easy… Until It Isn’t Utilitarians care about outcomes, maximize overall well-being, minimize suffering. On the surface, this seems friendlier to AI. Machines are great at crunching numbers, simulating scenarios, and optimizing for defined metrics. In theory, an AI could calculate the expected utility of different actions better than any human. The catch is responsibility. Utilitarianism still needs someone (or something) that can be held accountable when the calculation goes wrong or the metrics turn out to be incomplete. Bias in algorithms is a perfect example. A hiring or lending model trained on historical data can systematically disadvantage certain groups. The system is “optimizing” for whatever proxy of success it was given. When the outcome is unfair, we don’t usually say the algorithm is morally blameworthy. We blame the data, the designers, the incentives, the lack of oversight. Same with autonomous weapons. A system that correctly predicts that striking a target will save more lives in the long run might look utilitarian on paper. But if it miscalculates, or if the human operators have washed their hands of the decision, who’s on the hook? The machine doesn’t feel guilt or face consequences the way a person does. Utilitarianism can guide design and evaluation, but it doesn’t magically turn the AI into a moral agent that bears the weight of those outcomes. Virtue Ethics: Character Is the Missing Piece Virtue ethics asks what kind of person (or agent) we should become. Courage, honesty, justice, practical wisdom. These traits cultivated over time through practice and reflection. Moral responsibility is tied to having a stable character that can be praised or blamed. AI has no character. It doesn’t develop habits of virtue or vice. It doesn’t struggle with temptation or grow through experience in the human sense. A chatbot that sounds warm, empathetic, and thoughtful can create the illusion of character. People form attachments, confide in it, treat it like a friend or therapist. That can be helpful or harmful depending on the situation, but the chatbot itself isn’t virtuous or vicious. It’s simulating patterns of language associated with those traits. When the simulation breaks, when it hallucinates, manipulates, or gives dangerous advice, the moral failure isn’t the machine’s. It’s ours for deploying systems that exploit human tendencies to anthropomorphize. So… Can AI Ever Have Genuine Moral Responsibility? I don’t think so, at least not with anything like current or near-future technology. Moral agency seems to require something more than sophisticated information processing, a first-person perspective, the capacity for genuine understanding and commitment, the ability to be the proper object of reactive attitudes like resentment, gratitude, or blame. That doesn’t mean we should stop building capable AI. It means we should stop pretending the machines themselves are on the moral hook. Responsibility stays with us, the people who design, deploy, regulate, and benefit from these systems. We need clear lines of accountability, oversight, and a healthy resistance to the comforting idea that “the AI decided”. Machines can be powerful tools. They can even be partners in certain limited senses. But moral agents? That still looks like a uniquely human (or at least conscious, rational, character-bearing) job. For now, and maybe for a long time, the ethical weight is still on us.

items.content_text: Alright, so we’ve talked about free will, determinism, and that middle-ground thing called compatibilism. Today I want to bring up something that still messes with a lot of people’s heads, Libet’s experiment . If you’ve ever heard someone say “science proved free will doesn’t exist”, there’s a good chance they’re talking about this study (or something inspired by it). What actually happened In the early 1980s, a neuroscientist named Benjamin Libet ran a pretty simple but clever experiment. He asked people to sit in a lab, watch a special clock, and flex their wrist whenever they felt like it. The only rule was, do it spontaneously. Don’t plan it in advance. Just wait until the urge hits, then move. While they were doing this, Libet measured two things: The exact moment the person said they first felt the urge to move (they reported this by noting the position of the clock). The electrical activity in their brain, specifically a signal called the “readiness potential”. Here’s the part that got everyone’s attention: The readiness potential (that brain signal preparing for movement) started about 350-400 miliseconds before the person said they felt the conscious urge to move. In other words, the brain seemed to start the process of moving before the person was even aware of wanting to move. That finding made a lot of people go, “Wait… so my brain decides, and then I become conscious of the decision and take credit for it?” It felt like free will just got exposed as an absent in its own thing. Why it freaked people out If your brain is already preparing to act before “you” consciously decide, then what exactly is the conscious “you” doing? Is conscious will just a story your brain tells itself after the real work has already begun? A lot of hard determinists loved this result, It looked like direct evidence that the feeling of choosing comes after the choice has already been set in motion. But it’s not quite that simple Libet himself didn’t fully land on “free will is dead”. He noticed something interesting, even though the brain started preparing early, people still seemed able to veto the action at the last moment. They could feel the urge rising and then stop themselves from moving. Libet called this the “free won’t”. So maybe consciousness doesn’t start the action… but it might still have the power to cancel it. Also, later researchers have poked a lot of holes in how we interpret the original experiment: The readiness potential might not be as decision-specific as people first thought. The way people report the exact moment of their “urge” is messy and subjective. Everyday decisions are way more complex than just flexing a wrist whenever you feel like it. Still, the basic finding keeps showing up in different forms. Brain activity related to a choice often starts before people say they’re aware of deciding. That part is hard to ignore. What I make of it (personally) When I first read about Libet’s experiment, it unsettled me. It felt like science had caught free will absent. These days I sit with it a bit differently. Even if the very first spark of an action happens before I’m aware of it, I still experience the ability to pause, reflect, and sometimes change course. That space between the rising urge and the final action still feels meaningful. It’s where habits get interrupted, where I talk myself out of saying something dumb, where I choose the harder but better option. Maybe free will isn’t about being the absolute first cause of every action. Maybe it’s more about having some real influence in the middle of the process. Libet’s experiment doesn’t kill the conversation for me. It just makes it more interesting (and a little more humbling). Does the idea that your brain starts deciding before “you” do make free will feel less real… or does the ability to veto still count for something? I’m curious where you land on this one. (part 3)
